tasks.goal:
TASK: teach block mode to recognise two more Bash write forms before they run: `dd ... of=FILE` and `find DIR ... -delete` / `find DIR ... -exec rm ...`. The acceptance test is test/block-dd-find.test.mjs (read it first; it drives the real hook with PreToolUse payloads in a temp git repo whose fences are: no-migrations = deny block migrations/**, notes-warn = deny warn notes/**).

1. dd: any operand `of=FILE` (quotes already removed by words(), so `of="x"` arrives as `of=x`) is an 'edit' of FILE, in whatever position it appears. `if=FILE` is a read and must not become a target. dd without of= writes nothing.
2. find: the DIR operands are the positional words after `find` up to the first word that starts with `-`, `(` or `!` (several DIRs allowed; none means `.`). If the expression contains `-delete`, or `-exec`/`-execdir`/`-ok`/`-okdir` followed by a deleting command (rm, unlink, rmdir, shred; the command word may be a path like /bin/rm), then every DIR is a 'delete' target (the caller's expand() turns a directory into every repo file under it, so "everything find could match" is counted; `find . -delete` covers the whole repo). A find without -delete / -exec rm (e.g. `find migrations -name '*.sql'`, `-exec cat {} \;`, `find x | wc -l`) writes nothing. `cd` earlier in the command applies as for other targets.
3. Add unit cases for both to test/fences.test.mjs style in a NEW test file if you like (optional), but do not edit existing tests.

Check: `node --test test/block-dd-find.test.mjs` passes and `npm test` passes.
CONTEXT (fenceline, Node 18+, ES modules, zero dependencies; `npm test` runs `node --test test/*.test.mjs`). Fenceline is a Claude Code hook (hooks/fenceline-hook.mjs). On PreToolUse for the Bash tool it calls preDecision() in src/trail.mjs, which asks bashWriteTargets() in src/fences.mjs what files a shell command will write ([{file, op: create|edit|delete, cd}]), resolves each with relPath() + expand() (a directory expands to every repo file under it; '.' or '' is the whole repo), and denies the call if a write lands in a fence whose mode is "block". bashWriteTargets already reads redirections, rm/mv/cp/touch/tee, sed -i, git checkout/restore, VAR= prefixes, sudo/env/xargs wrappers and `cd` earlier in the same command (splitCommand() splits on ; && || | and newlines, words() splits a part into shell words with quotes removed). Edits made any other way are caught after the fact by PostToolUse, so block mode is best-effort and must never produce false denials for commands that only read.

RULES: Do not change or delete tests that already exist in test/ (including the acceptance test copied in for this task); read them, they define done. Keep every existing test passing (`npm test`). The hook must keep exiting 0 and must never crash: any error inside the hook is logged to $FENCELINE_HOME/hook-errors.log and the tests fail if that file appears, so guard file reads with try/catch. Prefer extending bashWriteTargets() in src/fences.mjs (and preDecision() in src/trail.mjs where a target needs the filesystem) so that both the hook and any CLI share one analysis. Keep the code style of the repo (compact, commented where the reasoning is not obvious). Do not run `claude` or anything that calls an LLM.

TASK: teach block mode to look inside a command wrapped in a shell: `sh -c '...'`, `bash -c "..."`, `/bin/sh -c ...`, `bash -lc ...` (any single-dash flag cluster containing `c`, e.g. -c, -lc, -ec, -xc; the script is the next word). The acceptance test is test/block-shell-wrap.test.mjs (read it first; it drives the real hook with PreToolUse payloads in a temp git repo whose fences are: no-migrations = deny block migrations/**, notes-warn = deny warn notes/**). The previous task added `dd of=` and `find -delete` / `find -exec rm` to bashWriteTargets() in src/fences.mjs; those must also be seen inside a wrapper.

How: in bashWriteTargets(), when the command word (after stripping sudo/env/... and a leading path) is sh, bash, zsh or dash and a `-c`-style flag is present, take the script word that follows the flag and analyse it with the same rules as the outer command (call bashWriteTargets recursively on it; the script is already unquoted by words(), so it is a plain command string like `echo x > migrations/001.sql` or `cd migrations && rm 001.sql`). Each inner target's `cd` must be combined with the outer `cd` in force at that point (inner cd relative to outer cd; if either is null the result is null). Only an actual wrapper command counts: `echo "sh -c 'rm x'" > notes/cmd.txt` is an echo whose argument merely contains the text, and must not be denied (word-level analysis gives this for free; do not regex-scan the raw string). A wrapped command that only reads (`sh -c 'cat migrations/001.sql'`) writes nothing. Guard against runaway recursion (depth limit ~4).

Check: `node --test test/block-shell-wrap.test.mjs` passes and `npm test` passes (which includes the earlier acceptance test test/block-dd-find.test.mjs).

TASK: teach block mode to see the files a patch touches before `git apply FILE`, `patch ... < FILE`, `patch ... -i FILE` / `--input=FILE` run, by reading the patch file's `---` / `+++` headers. The acceptance test is test/block-patch-apply.test.mjs (read it first; it drives the real hook with PreToolUse payloads in a temp git repo whose fences are: no-migrations = deny block migrations/**, notes-warn = deny warn notes/**; the repo holds patches under patches/ in both git style with a/ b/ prefixes and plain style with timestamps). Earlier tasks added dd/find and sh -c handling to bashWriteTargets() in src/fences.mjs; keep them working.

How (suggested): bashWriteTargets() is pure and does not touch the filesystem, so have it return a target like { patch: FILE, cd } for `git apply [flags] FILE` (the first positional after apply; skip --check/--stat/--numstat/--summary if you wish) and for `patch` when stdin is redirected from a file (`< FILE`, detached or attached as `<FILE`; note words() does not currently split `<`) or `-i FILE` / `--input=FILE` is given (also accept a second positional file as the patch file). Then in preDecision() in src/trail.mjs, for each such target resolve the patch file against path.resolve(cwd, t.cd) (absolute paths as given), read it with try/catch (a missing or unreadable file yields no targets and no error log), and collect the paths from every line starting with `--- ` and `+++ `: cut at the first tab (timestamps), skip `/dev/null`, strip a leading `a/` or `b/` (git style; plain headers have no prefix and are used as-is). Each path is a write: 'create' if the `---` side was /dev/null, 'delete' if the `+++` side was /dev/null, else 'edit'; resolve it with relPath against the directory the command runs in, like other targets. Reading the patch file itself (`cat patches/mig.patch`) or writing a patch file elsewhere (`git diff > patches/out.patch`) must not be treated as applying it; other git subcommands must stay as they are.

Check: `node --test test/block-patch-apply.test.mjs` passes and `npm test` passes (which includes the earlier acceptance tests test/block-dd-find.test.mjs and test/block-shell-wrap.test.mjs).

TASK: add a CLI command `fenceline check "<shell command>"` to bin/fenceline.mjs and update the README. The acceptance test is test/check-cli.test.mjs (read it first; it runs bin/fenceline.mjs with spawnSync inside a temp git repo whose fences are: no-migrations = deny block migrations/**, notes-warn = deny warn notes/**, secrets = deny block .env with reads: true; and it reads README.md).

1. `fenceline check "<cmd>"`: run inside a git repo (use the existing root() helper; outside a repo it already exits 2). Load the fences with loadFences(root) and the repo files with listFiles(root). Analyse the command exactly as the hook's PreToolUse does for the Bash tool, but against ALL fences (warn and block, not only block): the write targets from bashWriteTargets() in src/fences.mjs resolved and expanded as preDecision() in src/trail.mjs does (including the patch-file reading added in the previous task), plus a read counts for a fence with reads: true (bashReads() in src/trail.mjs, as the hook does). The cleanest way is to factor the Bash part of preDecision() into an exported function in src/trail.mjs, e.g. bashCrossings(command, { root, cwd, fences, exists, files }) -> crossings, and call it from both preDecision() (with the block fences) and the CLI (with all fences). Treat the command as run from the repo root. Print one line per crossing to stdout, each naming the fence id (for example `no-migrations  delete migrations/001.sql  [block]  "migrations: off-limits"`), de-duplicated per fence+file+op is fine; with no crossing print one short line such as `no fence crossed` that contains no fence id. Exit 1 if any crossing is against a fence whose mode is block, else 0. With no command argument print a usage line to stderr and exit 2.
2. Add `check` to the usage comment block at the top of bin/fenceline.mjs; note that the no-argument usage printout is produced by `.split('\n').slice(1, 11)` of that file, so widen the slice if your new comment line falls outside it (the test runs `fenceline` with no args and expects the word check in stdout, exit 0).
3. README.md: document `fenceline check "<cmd>"` (e.g. in the "Fences and the map" or "For the engineers" section) and rewrite the "## Limits" section so it no longer lists dd, find -delete, sh -c, git apply or patch as writes block mode cannot prevent: block mode now reads `dd … of=`, `find … -delete` / `-exec rm`, commands wrapped in a shell (`sh -c`, `bash -c`) and the headers of a patch given to `git apply` / `patch`. The Limits section (from `## Limits` to the next `## ` heading) must not contain the strings `dd of=`, `find -delete`, `sh -c` or `git apply` at all; describe what still slips through instead (scripts, `node -e`, `python -c`, `eval`, `xargs rm`, git commands that rewrite the tree, a patch whose headers do not name the file, a shell wrapper nested deeper than block mode follows). Also update the sentence in Limits that lists what block mode can read off the command line.

Check: `node --test test/check-cli.test.mjs` passes and `npm test` passes (which includes the three earlier acceptance tests).
